title: Noli me tangere
medium: Oil on canvas (sketch for an arched composition, 54 × 150.5 cm)
summary: In a pale, wooded garden, the risen Christ stands before the kneeling Mary Magdalene and gestures to her not to approach, while showing her the wounds of his Passion. Around them Denis unfolds the rest of Easter morning: Peter and John hurrying to the tomb, and the holy women addressed by two angels guarding the sepulchre. The soft, luminous colours and arched format reflect Denis's lifelong ambition to renew sacred art for churches of the modern age.
facts: In 1919, the year before this painting, Denis co-founded the Ateliers d'Art Sacré in Paris with George Desvallières to train artists for the decoration of churches.
The canvas, catalogued by the museum as a sketch (esquisse) with an arched top, was bequeathed to Reims by the art historian and curator Paul Jamot in 1939.
Several episodes of the Resurrection appear side by side in the one landscape, a narrative device that recalls early Italian painting, which Denis deeply admired.

title: Signs of Christ
location: International Centre of the Roerichs, Moscow, Russia
medium: Tempera on canvas (Google Arts & Culture lists oil)
summary: Among wind-rippled dunes of ochre sand beneath blue hills, a long-haired figure of Christ sits tracing mysterious signs in the sand with a staff, while a hooded companion bends over him to watch. Roerich, the Russian painter, mystic and explorer, was fascinated by legends of Christ's presence in Asia and painted him as a quiet wanderer in a timeless landscape. The flat, glowing colours give the scene the stillness of an icon.
facts: The painting belongs to Roerich's 'Banners of the East' series, which portrays teachers and prophets of many religions.
The painting is signed and dated 1924 at Talai-Pho-Brang, the house in Darjeeling where the Roerich family lived after arriving in India.
In 1925, during his Central Asian expedition, Roerich recorded legends in Ladakh about 'Issa' (Jesus) travelling in India, which he retold in his book Altai–Himalaya.

title: The Risen Christ (Der Auferstandene)
summary: A gaunt, beardless Christ sits half-length before an empty tomb, holding the banner of the Resurrection, his emaciated body marked by suffering rather than glorified. Egger-Lienz, who had witnessed the First World War as a war painter, made this stark figure the culmination of a four-part cycle in the district memorial chapel for the fallen of Lienz. It offers resurrection hope that does not look away from the cost of death.
facts: The unconventional image provoked fierce protests; on 5 May 1926 the Vatican placed the chapel under interdict, forbidding church services there for decades.
The press mocked the figure as 'consumptive'; the chapel was finally reconsecrated in June 1987. These are the only frescoes Egger-Lienz ever painted.
Egger-Lienz himself is buried in the chapel, which was dedicated on 8 September 1925 and designed by the architect Clemens Holzmeister.

title: The Reunion (Das Wiedersehen: Christ and Thomas)
location: Original wood carving: Hamburg (Reemtsma collection, Ernst Barlach Haus); bronze cast pictured: Osthaus Museum, Hagen, Germany
summary: Two long-robed figures meet in an embrace: the risen Christ, thin and upright, supports the doubting apostle Thomas, who sinks against him and gazes up into his face. Barlach reduces the Gospel encounter to two bodies and one gesture of recognition and mercy. It is one of the most tender works of German Expressionist sculpture.
facts: Barlach, also a playwright, was preoccupied with themes of doubt, longing and spiritual rebirth, which this sculpture embodies.

The wooden original was bought by the Schwerin state museum soon after it was carved, but was confiscated by the Nazis as 'degenerate art' in 1937; it later passed to the Hamburg collector Hermann F. Reemtsma.

The first bronzes, cast from a smaller plaster model, were made in 1930 for the Galerie Flechtheim in Berlin; further casts made after 1945 are in several collections, including the Neue Nationalgalerie, Berlin.

title: Ecce Homo
location: Ruins of St Michael's (old Coventry Cathedral), Coventry, UK
summary: A massive, block-like Christ stands bound, his heavy head and broad face confronting the viewer with silent endurance. Epstein carved the figure directly from a single block of marble, rejecting any sweet or idealised image of Jesus in favour of something monumental and primal. Today it stands in the bombed-out shell of Coventry's medieval cathedral, a witness to suffering and reconciliation.
facts: When first exhibited in 1935 it was attacked as ugly and even blasphemous, and it remained unsold for decades.
After Epstein's death, the sculpture was given to Coventry Cathedral at the wish of his widow, Lady (Kathleen) Epstein, and was dedicated in the ruins on 22 March 1969.
Epstein also made the large bronze St Michael's Victory over the Devil on the wall of the new Coventry Cathedral, as well as the aluminium Majestas in Llandaff Cathedral.

title: Cristo Blanco (White Christ)
artist: Attributed to Francisco Olazo Allende (some sources name Ernesto Olazo Allende)
location: Pukamuqu hill, near Sacsayhuamán, Cusco, Peru
medium: Granite faced with marble and plaster
summary: A white figure of Christ, arms outstretched in welcome and blessing, stands on a hill above the old Inca capital of Cusco. The statue overlooks the city from beside the great Inca walls of Sacsayhuamán, joining Andean and Christian landscapes in one view. It has become one of Cusco's best-loved landmarks.
facts: The statue was given to the city in 1945 by the community of Palestinian Arab Christians who had settled in Cusco, traditionally as a sign of gratitude.
It stands about 8 metres tall at an altitude of roughly 3,600 metres above sea level, and lies within the historic centre of Cusco inscribed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site.
Its open-armed pose recalls the larger Christ the Redeemer in Rio de Janeiro, completed in 1931.

title: The Life of Jesus (series of 30 paintings)
location: Seoul Museum, Buam-dong, Seoul, South Korea
medium: Ink and colour (traditional East Asian painting)
summary: Painted while Kim was a refugee during the Korean War, these thirty scenes retell the life of Christ from the Annunciation to the Ascension as if it had happened in Joseon-dynasty Korea. Jesus and the apostles wear white hanbok and horsehair gat hats, and Gospel events unfold among thatched villages and pine-clad hills. The series is a landmark of Korean Christian art and of Christian inculturation in East Asia.
facts: Kim, who lost his hearing in childhood, began the series in 1952 at his mother-in-law's house in Gunsan, where he had fled during the war.

He was encouraged by an American missionary, Anders K. Jensen, who argued that Koreans needed an image of Jesus that looked like them; Kim adapted traditional European Christian iconography to Korean settings.
In 1973 Kim painted the official standard portrait of King Sejong the Great, the image that has appeared on the South Korean 10,000-won banknote.
copyrightNote: © Estate of Kim Ki-chang. The series is held by the Seoul Museum in Buam-dong, Seoul.

title: The Sacrament of the Last Supper
location: National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C., USA
summary: Christ sits at a stone table before a calm bay, with twelve disciples bowed in prayer around him, while a vast transparent torso floats above with outstretched arms. The room is set within a huge, glass-like dodecahedron, a geometric figure that Plato associated with the cosmos. Dalí, who had returned to Catholicism, presents the Last Supper as a timeless, luminous sacrament rather than a dramatic meal.
facts: The landscape is the bay of Port Lligat, near Dalí's home on the Costa Brava.

The collector Chester Dale, who reputedly suggested the subject, bought it in 1956 and sent it to the National Gallery, where it went on view the day before Easter 1956; it formally entered the museum's collection as part of the Chester Dale Collection in 1963.
It became one of the most-viewed paintings at the National Gallery, even as critics debated its worth; the theologian Paul Tillich dismissed it as 'junk'.
copyrightNote: © Salvador Dalí, Fundació Gala-Salvador Dalí / Artists Rights Society. View it on the National Gallery of Art website.

title: Christ of Havana (Cristo de La Habana)
created: Carved in Rome, Italy; assembled in Havana, Cuba
location: Casablanca hill, overlooking Havana Bay, Cuba
summary: A towering white marble Christ stands on the hill of Casablanca, his right hand raised in blessing and his left on his heart, looking across the bay toward old Havana. The Cuban sculptor Jilma Madera carved the figure from Carrara marble in Italy, and it was assembled on site from 67 blocks, which had been blessed by Pope Pius XII before shipping. It was unveiled at Christmas 1958, just days before the Cuban Revolution triumphed.
facts: The statue was inaugurated on 24 December 1958; on 1 January 1959 Fulgencio Batista fled Cuba, and on 8 January Fidel Castro entered Havana.
The project is often said to have been promoted by Marta Fernández Miranda, wife of President Batista, in fulfilment of a vow.
Madera won the commission in 1953; the statue is about 20 metres tall including its 3-metre base and weighs roughly 320 tonnes.

title: Biblical stencil prints (katazome)
location: Impressions in many museum, university and church collections in Japan, the United States and Europe
medium: Hand-coloured stencil prints (katazome) on kozo and momigami paper
summary: Watanabe retold the Bible in the visual language of Japanese folk art: Christ and the apostles appear with round faces and almond eyes, dressed in kimono and, at the Last Supper, sharing sushi and sake, all framed in bold black lines and earthy reds, ochres and indigos. Using the traditional katazome stencil-dyeing technique, often on crumpled, cloth-like momigami paper, he gave scenes from the Nativity to the Passion a joyful, handmade warmth. His prints became beloved across the world as an image of the Gospel at home in Asian culture.
facts: Watanabe was baptized at seventeen and was deeply influenced by the mingei folk-craft movement of Yanagi Sōetsu and by the master dyer Serizawa Keisuke, from whom he learned the katazome stencil-dyeing technique.
Momigami, the paper he often printed on, is kneaded and crumpled by hand to give it a soft, cloth-like texture; his colours were bound with soybean milk prepared by his wife, Harue.
In 1958 his print The Bronze Serpent won first prize at the Modern Japanese Print Exhibition in New York, and his prints were especially beloved by churches and collectors in the United States.
copyrightNote: © Estate of Sadao Watanabe. Impressions can be viewed through museum collections in Japan and the United States.

title: The Last Supper (series)
location: Various collections, including the Andy Warhol Museum, Pittsburgh
medium: Synthetic polymer paint and silkscreen ink on canvas, and drawings
summary: In his final major body of work, Warhol reworked Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper again and again: as silkscreens, in camouflage patterns, overlaid with commercial logos, and as large hand-painted copies. Drawn from cheap reproductions of the mural, the series asks how a sacred image survives in a culture saturated with mass-produced pictures. Warhol, a quietly practising Byzantine Catholic, made some hundred works on the theme.
facts: The series was commissioned by the art dealer Alexander Iolas for an exhibition in Milan, across the street from Santa Maria delle Grazie, where Leonardo's original is painted.
The Milan exhibition opened in January 1987; Warhol died the following month, making it his last major show.
Warhol regularly attended Mass and volunteered at a homeless shelter, a side of his life that became widely known only after his death.
copyrightNote: © The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts / Artists Rights Society. View works from the series through the Andy Warhol Museum.
